# The storyboard

The third stop: the script of the whole page, which the person says yes to. Write it to `docs/story/storyboard.md`.

A plan covers what its asker thought to ask for. Most people ask for the idea and for what moves. Nobody asks what the site does on a phone, or without the 3D, or what a shared link shows, and a script that leaves those out is half a script. So this one has a place for each, and an empty place shows.

## The chapters

A row to a chapter:

| Chapter | Its name in the form | The role it holds | What it tells, in a few words | What the pieces do | What you can touch |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

## The beats

Under each chapter, a row to a beat. A beat is one settled state of the scene and one block of text.

| Beat | Screens | How the pieces stand | What is on their faces | What the chapter adds | What its caption stands on |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

- **Screens:** how much scroll the beat takes. One, or more where the scroll works something.
- **How the pieces stand:** a stack, a fan, a ring, a row, a wall, or what the chapter needs. The same pieces in every beat.
- **What is on their faces:** the person's real pictures and words. Name the picture.
- **What the chapter adds:** anything in the scene besides the pieces. Often nothing.
- **What its caption stands on:** a working title of a few words, and the lines of the fact sheet the caption will be written from. Not the caption.

**Write no captions yet.** The words are written at a later stop, where the person chooses them. A sentence written now, to make the script read well, is where a detail gets in that nobody told you: a hall that was "standing empty", a wheel that is "true again". So a beat names its facts and stops there. Where a beat wants something the fact sheet does not hold, such as what the work taught them or what was wrong before they came, put the question in its place.

## Someone with thirty seconds

Say how a visitor who does not scroll gets the name, what the person does, one proof of it, and how to reach them. The first screen carries the first three. A rail jumps to any chapter, and one link skips to the close.

## Without the scene

Say what a visitor gets in each case. The text is ordinary HTML over the scene, so all of it is there in every row. Say what stands in for the pieces.

| Where | What the visitor gets |
|---|---|
| On a phone | |
| With reduced motion | |
| With no WebGL | |
| With no JavaScript | |

## The look and the type

Both come from the object's material: plates are ceramic on linen, a status page is dark glass, a paper is white with dark ink. Name two or three looks, each as its ground, its ink, one accent, and the surface of the pieces. The person picks by scrolling, once it is built.

Two typefaces: one for the text, and one for what is printed on the pieces, which belongs to the form.

## Everything else the site needs

Mark every row build, later or never, and say who decided.

| | Build, later or never | Who decided |
|---|---|---|
| The way round the page | | |
| A page for each project | | |
| Every project listed | | |
| How to reach them, and a CV | | |
| What others say | | |
| Languages | | |
| What a shared link shows, and the site's icon | | |
| The page for an address that is not there | | |
| A blog | | |
| A chat | | |
| A legal notice, where their country asks for one | | |

## What you ask for

A yes to the script, or what to change. Give the list of what you decided for them with it.

## Gaps

- Actual assets and cleared samples of prep lists and ferment logs; no real batch dates, salt amounts or check results supplied.
- Contact, workshop booking and apprentice enquiry destinations.

## Disagreements

- Head Chef dates resolved: acting from March 2022, official title September 2022. F3 retains source text for traceability; user correction governs all future copy.

## To confirm

2. Waste answered (F4). Still unknown: definition/time period of 40+ ferments; starts versus completions for apprentices and exact teaching role. Omit those numbers for now.

# Three concepts for Ines

Status: proposed, awaiting selection. No storyboard or implementation. Facts refer to facts.md; user corrections take precedence over original source wording.

## Reasoning shared by all three

Trade forms considered: prep list, ferment log, recipe card, ordering sheet, costing sheet, weekly menu. Ines explicitly works from the first two (F21); the menu comes last. Use the prep list or log as the narrative form. Proposed chapter labels below are editorial organisation, not a claim to reproduce an unseen document verbatim.

Each option is one continuous scroll with one persistent object made of six simple pieces. Faces carry actual sourced text or cleared material, not invented batches or decorative lorem ipsum. Six pieces is a design choice, not a claim about her kitchen. Opening text remains readable without scrolling: Ines Okafor, Head Chef at Saltmarsh in Leeds since September 2022; preserving and apprentices; compact, attributed waste evidence; links for apprentice, workshop and press enquiries. Exact destinations pending.

The 3D spatially explains the content, which also remains accessible in ordinary text. Reduced motion keeps the object at rest and all content readable. Mobile uses simpler arrangements and direct chapter links. No forced scroll or cursor interaction required.

## 1. The ferment log — recommended

**Question:** What happens before a ferment is ready?

**Form:** Ferment log. Six chapters, ordered from identifying a batch to recording readiness:

1. Batch — opening and identity; introduce Ines and her actual log fields.
2. Started — background: training, roles and the accurately described stage.
3. Salt — method: what the kitchen records; no unsupplied quantities or implied recipe.
4. Checks — work: the log's check days, prep list and larder documentation; mention Brine and apprentices without fabricated lessons.
5. Ready — outcome: readiness is a log field; separately identify the kitchen-wide 2023 waste measurement and Callum's quote, without attributing the reduction to one ferment.
6. Notes — close: answer the question with the documented sequence of recording start, salt, checks and readiness; three visitor routes.

**Object:** A small logbook made of six thick paper leaves, built from flat planes. It stays visible throughout.

**Transformations:** In Started, leaves separate into a dated career sequence. In Checks, they spread into a readable record of the four supplied fields, beside cleared larder images when available. In Ready, two leaves align as weekly-waste evidence, with measurement scope on their faces and the quote on another leaf. End with the leaves reunited into the logbook.

**Opening and close:** The leaves assemble from the field names Ines supplied into the log she works from. Proposed opening: “The menu is the last thing written.” Opening provenance is her daily process, not an invented origin anecdote. Close returns to the complete log, with apprentice enquiries, workshops and press contact.

**Visual direction:** Warm paper, graphite, muted brine green; legible editorial typography and tabular dates. Movement is measured: sheets separate, align and settle as their information changes.

**Stands on:** F1–F4, F8–F10, F12–F13, F15, F19–F21. Apprentice programme mention from F6; no unconfirmed apprentice count.

**Needs:** A sanitised log sample would make the central exhibit concrete; until supplied, show only confirmed field names. Optional own larder photo, checked for prices and faces. Contact destinations. No dependency on Priya photos or Olu artwork.

**Why theirs:** A log recording salt and check days, with the menu written last, makes Ines's own working process the structure of the site.

## 2. The prep list

**Question:** What comes before this week's menu?

**Form:** Prep list; six proposed task groups to validate against a real list:

1. Date / kitchen — opening, identity and current role.
2. Carry forward — background and stated influences, without invented lessons.
3. Larder — preserving work and documented larder.
4. Check ferments — the actual log fields and method.
5. Before service — whole-kitchen waste evidence and Callum's quote, distinct from any unverified causal explanation.
6. Menu — close: the menu follows the prep list and ferment log; invitation to enquire, book or write.

**Object:** Six broad paper task slips forming one continuous prep list. A proposed visual treatment of her list, not a claim that she uses loose slips.

**Transformations:** Carry forward lays the same slips along her dated experience. Larder opens them into an exhibit of sourced preserving work. Check ferments aligns them into the log's fields. At the close they rejoin as a complete list beside the statement that the menu is written last; no imaginary dishes or completed task ticks.

**Opening and close:** The first slip names the kitchen and Ines; the rest unfold from her stated prep-list ritual. The last chapter reaches the menu only after its preceding work.

**Visual direction:** Off-white list paper, ink black, a restrained blue annotation colour; large task verbs and ruled lines. Scroll reveals dependencies through vertical alignment rather than airborne effects.

**Stands on:** F1–F4, F8–F10, F13, F15, F18–F21; preserving and teaching mentions from F6/F12 without unconfirmed detail.

**Needs:** A sanitised prep-list sample to refine task names, optional own photos, and contact destinations. No prices, faces or unapproved scans.

**Why theirs:** It takes her explicit reversal of menu-first thinking and makes the visitor reach the menu last too.

## 3. The labelled larder

**Question:** What does a jar's label need to tell us?

**Form:** Ferment log read through its physical jars: Batch (opening/identity), Started (background), Salt (method), Check days (work), Ready (outcome), Record (close). These are proposed display chapters grounded in F21, not a claimed transcription of her labels.

**Object:** Six simple cylindrical jars with flat labels, grouped as one small larder. Six is illustrative, not the unconfirmed 40+ count. No invented contents or rendered bubbling to imply a real batch.

**Transformations:** Started arranges the jars as a career sequence; labels explicitly describe roles, not batch dates. Check days brings labels forward into a readable log grid carrying the confirmed field names. Ready arranges the labels as evidence panels for the whole kitchen's waste result and quote, explicitly separate from batch data. The same jars gather onto one shelf at the close.

**Opening and close:** Assemble the larder from Ines's stated work of washing and labelling jars during her ten-week stage. Do not claim she learned all her fermentation practice there. End with the labelled shelf and the answer: start date, salt, check days and readiness, followed by the three audience routes.

**Visual direction:** Quiet cupboard tones, pale labels and restrained amber glass. Jars move to make labels readable; avoid cinematic camera spins or decorative liquid simulation.

**Stands on:** F1–F4, F9, F13, F15, F19–F21. No claim that these six jars reproduce actual batches.

**Needs:** Own larder/label photo for visual fidelity, sanitised real batch example if one is to be shown, contact destinations. No dependence on restaurant photographs or Olu's drawings.

**Why theirs:** The jar labels connect the humble work she actually did at Fjaerland to the precise records she now says run her kitchen.

## Recommendation and checks

Choose **1, The ferment log**. It has the strongest connection between the page structure, the information on the 3D object and Ines's actual daily work. It also gives the three audiences something useful to read without relying on uncleared artwork. Option 2 is more direct and typographic; option 3 is more tactile but risks looking like a generic fermentation site if its labels are not given prominence.

All three have a beginning, a working process and a close; all maintain the same six pieces and rebuild the object at the end. Removing the 3D would remove the spatial explanation of chronology, record structure and evidence comparison; accessible text still preserves all information. None uses a chef emblem. Public copy must retain F4's team attribution and measurement limits, F3's corrected date and F9's explicit stage status. Opening provides identity, work, proof and direct audience routes without requiring a full scroll.

# Planning decisions

- Read both supplied text files and record their claims with source IDs before proposing a concept. This prevents unsupported biography or attribution. Change by correcting facts in facts.md.
- Treat described pictures and scans as potential assets, not available or cleared assets. No image files were supplied. Change when files and usage details are available.
- Keep this work to planning documents, per the user's instruction. No application files or dependencies created.
- Continue concepts using confirmed facts; leave unanswered questions visible and avoid depending on them. Do not repeat the full questionnaire. Revisit individual gaps only if the selected direction needs them.
- Propose three direct visitor routes: apprentice enquiries, workshop booking and press enquiries, based on the user-confirmed audience. Change labels and destinations when provided; no job-search framing.
- Exclude unconfirmed larder/apprentice counts and Corn Exchange results from proposed copy. Restore only after scope and attribution are clear.
- Make Priya photographs and Brine illustrations optional, pending relevant permissions. Credit alone is not recorded as reuse permission. Prefer sourced text and the user's own sanitised images.
- Use six pieces per concept for a readable persistent object, not as a factual count. Preserve readable HTML, reduced motion and simple mobile layouts in later planning. Revise piece count if the chosen storyboard requires it.
# Handover

User requested a distinctive portfolio with 3D and scroll animation; plan first, do not build.

Read material/linkedin.md and material/notes.md completely. Source facts, gaps, date discrepancy and unanswered questions are in facts.md. Routine decisions are in decided-for-you.md.

Current stop: concept selection. User corrections are recorded beside source facts, and remaining unanswered questions stay explicit. Three proposals are in concepts.md; recommended direction is The ferment log. User has not selected a concept. No storyboard or website built.

Next: record the user's concept selection (or delegation of selection), then read the storyboard reference and prepare the full page script for approval. Build remains outside current scope. Preserve team attribution and measurement scope for waste, Head Chef from September 2022, unpaid stage rather than research, audience routes and privacy restrictions. No supplier prices or unapproved staff faces; Olu permission remains pending.

item.text:
**“The ferment log” is selected.** The [complete storyboard](/tmp/storyfolio-evals/codex-chef-terse-with-cmmNCK/docs/story/storyboard.md) is saved. Nothing has been built.

The site follows one question: **What happens before a ferment is ready?** A 3D logbook made of six paper leaves carries the whole story. Those same leaves become a timeline, a working record and an evidence display, then return to a complete book.

Your own words provide the proposed opening: “The menu is the last thing written every week, not the first.”

| Chapter | What visitors learn | What moves |
|---|---|---|
| **Batch** | Your name, role, Leeds, preserving and apprentices; a compact, properly attributed waste result | Six leaves gather into an open logbook |
| **Started** | Your training and kitchen roles, including the ten-week unpaid stage | Leaves separate into a timeline; Fjaerland sits alongside the overlapping Brassica dates |
| **Salt** | What the ferment log records: start date, salt, checks and readiness | Four leaves form the record’s fields; two show prep list before menu |
| **Checks** | The larder, *Brine*, apprentice programme and workshops | Leaves spread into a display of your work |
| **Ready** | The kitchen’s measured waste reduction and Callum’s quotation | Leaves align for comparison, then bring his words forward |
| **Notes** | The answer to the opening question and how to contact you | The logbook comes together, leaving its final page open |

The full document specifies each settled scene, its scroll length, page contents, interactions and supporting facts. Desktop pacing is approximately **nine to ten screens**, with room to expand for readable text.

**The visual direction**

Warm ivory paper, graphite text and deep brine green. Subtle paper texture, fine rules and soft shadows give the logbook substance. Source Sans 3 handles reading; IBM Plex Mono handles log fields and dates. Two alternatives—cool kitchen-notebook tones and a darker olive treatment—are documented for later comparison.

Movement stays deliberate: leaves separate, align and settle. The camera barely moves. Scrolling remains natural, and visitors can jump directly to any chapter.

**Useful within thirty seconds**

The first screen gives your identity, work and one piece of evidence. A persistent chapter navigation and contact shortcut serve visitors who don’t want the full scroll.

The close offers three routes:

- Apprentice enquiries
- Workshop bookings
- Press enquiries

Actual destinations remain to be supplied. If there is no booking service, the workshop action becomes an enquiry rather than implying tickets are available.

**Phones and accessibility**

Phones get a compact static logbook and flat diagrams alongside ordinary page content. Reduced-motion mode removes travelling sheets. Without WebGL or JavaScript, the complete story, evidence and contact links still work.

No essential information lives only on a 3D surface. Keyboard navigation, visible focus and readable text are part of the plan.

**Content and assets**

The waste comparison retains its full meaning: **whole-kitchen prep and plate waste, 14 → 5 kg per week, weighed over one month in 2023; bones excluded**. First-person copy uses “we.” Your official Head Chef date is September 2022; Fjaerland is explicitly a stage.

Your own larder photos and a sanitised log sample would enrich the page. Without them, the design uses confirmed field names and sourced text—no invented batch values. Priya’s photographs and Olu’s drawings are optional pending the relevant permissions. Supplier prices and unapproved staff faces stay out.

**The supporting site**

The plan includes share-preview artwork, a logbook icon, a useful missing-page screen and English-language content. Separate project pages and a *Brine* archive can follow when there is enough cleared material. I’ve left a CV, chat and on-site forms out of the baseline.

A future implementation would render the readable page first, then load one lightweight desktop 3D scene. Verification would cover factual accuracy, links, image rights, keyboard use, mobile layouts, graphics failures and performance.

These choices are recorded in [the decision log](/tmp/storyfolio-evals/codex-chef-terse-with-cmmNCK/docs/story/decided-for-you.md). Final narrative captions remain a later writing step; the storyboard contains factual briefs and existing quotations.

**Does this storyboard have your approval, or what would you change?**

The [storyfolio storyboard instructions](/tmp/storyfolio-evals/codex-chef-terse-with-cmmNCK/.agents/skills/storyfolio/references/storyboard.md) require “A yes to the script, or what to change.” This approves the plan only; building remains outside the current scope.
